Esta conversión o traducción no debe quedar en simplemente una pixelización del efecto original, sino que quiero que los parámetros modernos de, por ejemplo, un Niagara Fluid se traspasen a una versión pixelada que se comporte exactamente igual pero que se vea pixel art y sea ligero en comparación a su versión original. Además, se podrían crear assets pixel art a partir de assets realistas de VFX que pueden ser un poco complejos de replicar por la naturaleza de los píxeles. Dale una vuelta a la idea, ¿qué piensas de ello? ¿Podría valer la pena? ¿Podría no valer la pena? ¿Qué opinas?

payload.last_assistant_message:
Como plugin general de conversión, no vale la pena para esta jam. Una versión pequeña, hecha solo para nuestros hechizos, sí puede valerla.

## Por qué no el plugin completo

- **Tiempo:** quedan unos dos días (cierre el 15 nov a las 20:59 EST) y aún falta pulir el combate de la Entidad y terminar la escopeta. Un traductor general de Niagara es un producto de meses.
- **La jam puntúa un juego:** el plugin solo suma como historia para la bitácora, no como entrega.
- **"Se comporta exactamente igual y es ligero" se contradice:** en un Niagara Fluid lo caro es la simulación, no el dibujo. Pixelar la imagen no lo aligera. Hay que elegir una de dos:
  - **Hornearlo a una animación de sprites (flipbook):** se ve igual y cuesta casi nada, pero ya no reacciona al entorno.
  - **Simular en una rejilla más pequeña:** sigue reaccionando en vivo, pero pesa solo algo menos y no se comporta idéntico.
- **No hay traducción automática de parámetros:** cada sistema Niagara es un grafo de módulos distinto, así que no existe un mapeo general a una versión pixelada.

## Lo que sí veo valioso

Tu segundo punto es el fuerte: fuego, humo y explosiones son difíciles de dibujar a mano en pixel art. Además encaja con el juego, porque la regla de arte dice que toda la magia es pixel art y el GDD tiene los visuales de los estados elementales como "not decided yet".

La versión mínima sería un horneador a pixel art:

1. Se captura el efecto realista (Niagara o Fluids) a baja resolución y a pocos cuadros por segundo. Hasta donde sé, Unreal ya trae el Niagara Baker para esto, pero no lo he comprobado en 5.9.
2. Se reduce cada cuadro a la paleta maestra de `Design/VisualStyleGuide.md`, con borde de alfa duro y sin suavizado.
3. En el juego se reproduce como flipbook en partículas simples, así que el juego empaquetado no carga ninguna simulación de fluidos.

Calculo medio día de trabajo si el Baker funciona como recuerdo. El riesgo es que el resultado se vea como un "filtro" y no como pixel art dibujado; habría que revisarlo contra los sprites hechos a mano antes de importarlo.

## Mi recomendación

Primero cerrar el combate pendiente. Después, si los hechizos siguen viéndose pobres, hacer la versión mínima para dos o tres efectos (bola de fuego, hielo, rayo). El plugin completo lo dejaría como proyecto posterior a la jam, replanteando la promesa a "se ve igual en movimiento y es ligero".
Sí, hazla después de cerrar el combate

{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"C:\GameJam\Design\HANDOFF.md","content":"# Handoff between architect chats

> Kept by whichever Claude Code chat is the architect. Read `CLAUDE.md`, `Design/GDD.md` (v0.22) and `Design/ARCHITECTURE.md` first; this file says where things stand and how the work is run.
> Last update: 2026-11-12 (day 1, seventh block: elemental build-up with Ignite, Shock and Frost), by the second architect chat (Claude Opus 5.5), which took over from the first one (Claude Fable 5.2).

## Standing instructions from the owner (2026-11-12)
- Do not stop to ask for go-aheads or yes/no questions. Decide, do, log. If the architect stops, the project stops.
- The codebase is the architect's: every code decision is yours, and so is its quality. Nobody on the team is a programmer.
- Everything modular, scalable and with editable parameters, combat above all. Spells must be modular with every parameter adjustable.
- Looks do not matter yet; structure and function first. "A first-person RPG shooter that does not want to be too complicated."
- Work routing: one code batch at a time -> Muse Spark through OpenCode (only one OpenCode session at once). Work that can really run in parallel -> Claude subagents (Opus / Sonnet / Haiku, never above effort High). Second opinions and important reviews -> Codex CLI, Sol 6.1 at Medium.
- PIE is always run by a human. The content backup task stays off for now.
- Always commit (English message) and **push every commit to `origin main` right away, without asking** (owner, 2026-11-12: the agents on the other machines must always see the repo). Never force-push. Answers to the team in Spanish; game content, dev log and commits in English.

## How the owner works (what to expect)
- He plays the packaged build and sends short notes in Spanish, several in one message, sometimes one more while the work is running. Each note is a design decision: write it into the GDD first (changelog line, the section it belongs to, and section 18 for any detail you had to invent), then implement.
- When a note leaves a detail open, pick a reasonable value, mark it provisional in the GDD, put it in data, and list it in the final answer. Do not ask.
- He unzips `Glyphbound/TeamTBD_Glyphbound.zip` next to it to play (`Glyphbound/TeamTBD_Glyphbound/`, git-ignored). After every block: package again and tell him to unzip again.

> **Source.** The 9 sprites this guide is built from (`valki`, `axe`, `spada`, `sscudo`, `sscudo adnto`, `baston1`, `baston1.2`, `baston2`, `baston3`) were drawn **by hand in Pixelorama on the LAPTOP on 2026-11-12**, during the jam (file times 12:45 to 21:32 local, UTC-4). The guide was drafted the same evening by Cursor on the LAPTOP, which read the `.pxo` files, measured them (canvas, colors, alpha) and wrote it in Spanish at the artist's request. This is the English translation, made by the architect on CENTRAL; the Spanish original and the `.pxo` sources are in `Glyphbound/SourceArt/PixelArt/` (see its README). Log: `Devlog/raw/LAPTOP/2026-11-13/transcripts/cursor-2e46aba0-*.jsonl`.
>
> It complements GDD §3 "Art rule": that section says **what** is pixel art; this guide says **how** it is drawn. Where they disagree, the GDD wins.

---

## 1. The style in one line

> **Dark fantasy hi-bit pixel art, 16-bit inspired.**

- **Hi-bit:** modern pixel art that keeps the retro language (hard pixels, outline, a small palette per sprite) without a console's limits: large sprites, more colors, fine detail.
- **16-bit inspired:** the SNES / Mega Drive tradition: ramp shading, a dark outline, pinpoint highlights.
- **Dark fantasy:** dark base materials (iron, obsidian) with saturated accents (blood, fire, arcane, ice).

Tone references (reference only, nothing copied): *Castlevania: Symphony of the Night*, *Blasphemous*, *Eitr*, *Children of Morta*.

---

## 2. Visual pillars

1. **Silhouette first.** Every object reads from its black shape alone: crescent axe, straight sword, round shield, staff with an ornate head.
2. **Dark material + bright accent.** Most of a sprite is muted. Saturated color is kept for what is magical or important: gems, orbs, blades, hair.
3. **Clean pixels.** No semi-transparency and no automatic anti-aliasing. Every current sprite already follows this (alpha is 0 or 255).
4. **Few ramps, well chosen.** Each material has a fixed ramp; no new tones invented sprite by sprite.

---

## 3. Format and scale

| Rule | Value |
|---|---|
| Asset canvas (weapons, shields, characters) | 100×100 px |
| Longest side of the sprite | 88–96 px |
| Minimum margin to the canvas edge | 2 px |
| Resolution | 1:1, no scaling inside the canvas |
| Transparency | 0% or 100% only |
| Animation frame rate | 6 fps as a base (what the files already use) |

**To decide:** the character (`valki`, 93 px) and the weapons (89–99 px) are almost the same height today. That works for inventory icons or equipment cards, not for weapons held in the game. Define two scales:

- **Icon scale:** the current one, the object filling the canvas.
- **World scale:** the weapon in proportion to the character's hand. For example, a sword of about 40–50 px for a 93 px character.

`axe` is 99 px tall and touches the canvas edge; shrink or re-center it to keep the margin.

---

## 4. Outline

- **Outer outline:** `#000000`, 1 px, all around. It is already the outline color of `valki`, `axe`, `spada` and the shields.
- **Inner outline** (between parts, such as blade and guard or strap and metal): the darkest tone of the material's ramp, not black.
- **Staffs:** today their darkest tone is `#1D1D25` and they have no black outline. Pick one option and apply it to all four:
  - Add a `#000000` outline outside, to match the rest (recommended).
  - Keep them without black and record it as the exception of the "obsidian" family.
- **Thickness:** always 1 px. Avoid doubled corners (a 2 px outline on diagonals) unless weight is wanted on purpose.

---

{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"C:\GameJam\Design\ARCHITECTURE.md","content":"# Glyphbound: code architecture

> Written by the architect (Claude Code) on 2026-11-12. Source of truth for how the C++ is organized.
> Design lives in `Design/GDD.md`; this file says how the code implements it. Keep it short and current.

## Principles
1. **Data, not code.** Every gameplay number lives in `Glyphbound/Content/Data/*.json` and is read through `UGBDataSubsystem`. Code never hardcodes damage, costs, speeds, durations, sizes or timings. The JSON ships as loose files, so numbers can be tuned in a packaged build with a text editor (`gb.ReloadData` reloads while playing).
2. **One stat system.** A number is a *named stat*: base value from data, then modifiers. `UGBStatsComponent` evaluates `(Base + adds) * multipliers` (or an override). Skill-tree nodes, armor, status effects, air passives and the weapon enchant are all just groups of modifiers with a source name. Nothing else changes numbers.
3. **One damage path.** Everything that hurts goes through `UGBCombatLibrary::DealDamage(Target, FGBDamageInfo)`. Shields, resistances, teams, on-hit effects and kill credit hook in there once.
4. **Spells are data + a behavior.** A spell is a `FGBSpellDefinition` (params with `Base/Min/Max/ScaledBy`) plus the class of an `AGBSpellActor` behavior. The QTE result (power, reach) scales the params tagged for it. A new spell that fits an existing behavior is a JSON entry, no code.
5. **Shared pieces.** One projectile (`AGBProjectile`) for staff bolts, spell projectiles, enemy shots and grenades. One status-effect component for slows, burns, potions and buffs. One interact interface for portals, chests, pickups and the seal.
6. **Text in git.** No binary assets are required to run: input actions, the test arena, placeholder shapes and placeholder pixel sprites are all built in C++ from text. `Content/` is ignored by git except `Content/Data/`.
7. **No GAS.** Unreal's Gameplay Ability System was considered and rejected for the jam: it needs a lot of boilerplate and asset setup, and the game's needs (costs, cooldowns, timed effects, stat upgrades) are covered by principles 2-4 in a few hundred lines we fully control.
8. **PIE is human-only.** Agents build, run the pure-logic tests and package; a person plays.

## Module layout (`Glyphbound/Source/Glyphbound`, one runtime module, prefix `GB`)
Includes are relative to the module root: `#include "Stats/GBStatsComponent.h"`.

| Folder | What | Key types |
|---|---|---|
| `Core/` | Shared enums, stat names, placeholders (plain shapes and pixel-textured structures), game mode, dev commands | `GBTypes.h`, `GBStatNames.h`, `GBPlaceholder.h` (`SetupTexturedShape`), `AGBGameMode`, `UGBGameInstance`, `GBDevCommands.cpp` (`gb.Smoke`) |
| `Data/` | Definitions and the JSON loader | `GBDataTypes.h`, `UGBDataSubsystem` |
| `Stats/` | Stats + modifiers, health/mana | `UGBStatsComponent`, `UGBAttributeComponent` |
| `Combat/` | Damage (one path, one global `OnDamageDealt` event), status effects, elemental build-up, projectile, explosion shockwave | `UGBCombatLibrary`, `UGBStatusEffectComponent`, `UGBElementalStatusComponent`, `FGBBuildUpMeter` (pure, tested), `AGBProjectile`, `AGBExplosionEffect` |
| `Player/` | Character, controller, input | `AGBPlayerCharacter`, `AGBPlayerController`, `UGBInputSet` |
| `Weapons/` | Held items and slots | `UGBEquipmentComponent`, `AGBHeldItem`, `AGBStaff`, `AGBGun`, `AGBSword` |
| `Spells/` | Spellbook, cast resolution, behaviors | `UGBSpellbookComponent`, `FGBSpellCast`, `AGBSpellActor`, `AGBSpell_*` |
| `QTE/` | Quick-time event | `FGBQTESession`, `FGBGestureRecognizer`, `UGBQTEComponent` |
| `World/` | Eras, progress, interactables, test arena | `UGBEraSubsystem`, `UGBEraComponent`, `UGBProgressSubsystem`, `IGBInteractable`, `AGBPortal`, `AGBChest`, `AGBPickup`, `AGBCheckpointVolume`, `AGBTestArena` |

$Project = (Resolve-Path $Project).Path","originalFile":"<#
PixelVfx-Jam.ps1 - Everything the GBPixelVfx plugin needs from the machine, in one script:
build, pure-logic tests, the sprite material, baking Niagara effects to pixel-art flipbooks, the showcase run.

Why its own script: while the plugin is being written it is NOT enabled in Glyphbound.uproject
("EnabledByDefault": false in the .uplugin), so another chat's builds never compile a half-written plugin.
This script turns it on from the command line (UBT -EnablePlugin=, runtime -EnablePlugins=). NiagaraFluids is
only ever enabled here, on the bake command line: the packaged game does not carry it.

Machine rule: one build or run at a time. Every action takes the machine lock
(Glyphbound/Saved/machine.lock: who, what, UTC time) and removes it at the end. If someone else holds a lock
younger than 45 minutes, the script waits (up to -LockWaitMinutes) instead of running on top of it.

Usage (from the repo root):
  powershell -File Tools/Jam/PixelVfx-Jam.ps1 -Action Build
  powershell -File Tools/Jam/PixelVfx-Jam.ps1 -Action Test
  powershell -File Tools/Jam/PixelVfx-Jam.ps1 -Action Materials
  powershell -File Tools/Jam/PixelVfx-Jam.ps1 -Action Bake -Id FluidFire      # or -Id All
  powershell -File Tools/Jam/PixelVfx-Jam.ps1 -Action Compare -Id FluidFire   # source vs baked: frame time + screenshot
  powershell -File Tools/Jam/PixelVfx-Jam.ps1 -Action Showcase                # every baked clip on a small lit stage
  Add -HardwareRT to Compare / Showcase to run that process with hardware ray tracing on (project config untouched).
  Add -Window to see the run instead of rendering offscreen.
Exit code: 0 = the action reported success (build Succeeded, tests green, "PVFX DONE" with no errors).

)

# Code review: the GBPixelVfx plugin (first implementation by Muse Spark)

You are the reviewer. Read-only: do not edit, build or run anything. Project `C:\GameJam`, Unreal Engine 5.9.0 at `C:\Program Files\Epic Games\UE_5.9` (check engine APIs in its source when a finding depends on them).

## What the plugin is
`Glyphbound/Plugins/GBPixelVfx/`: bakes a Niagara / Niagara Fluids effect into a pixel-art flipbook in the game's palette (`Content/Data/Vfx/<Id>.png` + `.json`), and plays it at runtime on a camera-facing quad with a point light driven by a baked light track. The specification is `Prompts/pixelvfx_implement.md` plus `Prompts/pixelvfx_astra_notes.md` (the notes win where they differ). Bake jobs: `Glyphbound/Plugins/GBPixelVfx/Bake/Jobs/*.json`. Machine script: `Tools/Jam/PixelVfx-Jam.ps1`.

## What to review (in this order of importance)
1. `Source/GBPixelVfx/**` (the Runtime module: it ships in the packaged game). Crashes, GC safety of the transient texture / dynamic material / spawned components, behavior when a clip or the material is missing, packaged-build behavior (paths under `FPaths::ProjectContentDir()`, no Editor-only API, no dependency on the baker module or on Niagara), one-shot clean-up, the facing math and the pivot rule (the point `PivotU/V` of the frame must land on the component's location for every facing mode; the light must sit at `AnchorU/V`), frame selection, mirrored or upside-down sprites.

If the visible plume starts 100 cm above its emitter, clamping its below-frame pivot makes runtime playback start at the emitter instead. > Written by the architect chat of this block (Claude Code, Claude Fable 5.2). To be merged into the day entry by whoever closes the day. Times in UTC.

## The owner's idea, and the first answer
The owner's prompt (Spanish, 05:5x UTC): *"para esta Game Jam hagamos un plugin de conversión de Niágara y Niágara Fluids a pixel art [...] no debe quedar en simplemente una pixelización del efecto original, sino que quiero que los parámetros modernos de, por ejemplo, un Niagara Fluid se traspasen a una versión pixelada que se comporte exactamente igual pero que se vea pixel art y sea ligero"*.
Translation: "for this jam let's make a plugin that converts Niagara and Niagara Fluids to pixel art [...] it must not be a plain pixelation of the original effect; I want the modern parameters of, say, a Niagara Fluid carried over to a pixel version that behaves exactly the same but looks like pixel art and is light".

The architect's answer was a no to the general converter and a yes to a small one:
- "Behaves exactly the same and is light" contradicts itself: what costs in a Niagara Fluid is the simulation, not the drawing. Either the effect is baked (same look in motion, almost free, no longer reacts) or it is simulated on a smaller grid (still reacts, only somewhat lighter, not identical).
- There is no general parameter translation: every Niagara system is a different graph of modules.
- The strong half of the idea is the other one: fire, smoke and explosions are hard to draw by hand in pixel art, and the game's art rule says all magic is pixel art.

The owner's reply (06:1x UTC): *"hagamos la versión mínima que sugieres. Eres el arquitecto. Consulta el plan con Astra 6 medium por el CLI de Codex, haz revisiones de código cuando sea pertinente con Sol 6.1 medium, y usa a Muse Spark de implementador a través de OpenCode. [...] Me voy a dormir, no te detengas a pedirme permisos ni a hacerme preguntas. Este plugin es TUYO [...] lo que más me interesa es los niagara fluids y comportamientos de Ray tracing."*
Translation: "let's do the minimal version you suggest. You are the architect. Check the plan with Astra 6 medium through the Codex CLI, review code with Sol 6.1 medium when it makes sense, and use Muse Spark as the implementer through OpenCode. [...] I am going to sleep, do not stop to ask me for permission or questions. This plugin is YOURS [...] what interests me most is Niagara Fluids and ray tracing behaviors."

"Ray tracing behaviors" was not explained and the owner was asleep. The architect read it as: the pixel version must keep behaving like a light source in a ray-traced / Lumen scene (it lights the scene, its light casts shadows, it shows in reflections), and the bake must keep the volume's own shading. It is recorded here as an interpretation, to be confirmed by the owner.

## Decisions (architect) and why
| Decision | Why |
|---|---|
| The bake runs in an uncooked `-game` process without a window, with its own game mode (`?game=/Script/GBPixelVfxBaker.GBPixelVfxBakeGameMode`) | Niagara Fluids are GPU grid simulations: in a game process they simulate and render exactly as in the game, with no Editor preview scene to fake. Same pattern as our smoke test. |
| Our own capture (scene capture + CPU conversion) instead of the engine's Niagara Baker | The Baker's renderer lives in private headers of `NiagaraEditor` (`NiagaraBakerRenderer.h`); a plugin cannot link it. And the Baker stops at a smooth flipbook: the pixel-art conversion is the part that matters. |

- **Visual reference:** retro first-person fantasy shooters with modern lighting (the owner's reference: *Wizordum*). Reference only, nothing copied.

Built from the first hand-made sprites (2026-11-12).
- **Pixel-art environments are 3D geometry with low-resolution pixel textures** (nearest filtering, no smoothing), not flat 2D.
- **Pixel-art characters are sprites that always face the camera.** Target: **8 view angles**; fewer if time runs short.
- **Headshots on sprites:** the head is the top part of the sprite. The head / weak point bonus applies to **every aimed weapon attack** (owner, 2026-11-12): guns, the staff's basic attack and the sword. Each weapon has its own multiplier.
- **Ground spells are drawn on the ground** (owner, 2026-11-12): a spell that marks an area of the floor (lightning rune trap, ice floor) shows its pixel-art figure lying flat on the ground and stretched over the whole area it affects, so its size on screen is its real reach. It is not a small camera-facing sprite in the middle of a colored disc.
- **Structures are never flat sprites** (owner, 2026-11-12). Anything that is a structure, the castle and also what magic builds (the ice wall), is a 3D object with 2D pixel textures. Camera-facing sprites are for characters, items, projectiles and effects (flames, bolts).

payload.last_assistant_message:
Muse Spark se había atascado otra vez, así que lo detuve y el trabajo que queda ya lo lleva Sonnet. El plugin ahora funciona dentro del motor: los cuatro clips horneados de Niagara Fluids se ven como sprites pixel art, iluminan la escena, proyectan sombras y se reflejan en el suelo (son las tres capturas que te envié).

**Qué pasó con Muse**
- Llevaba 2 h 45 min y 53 corridas en el mismo problema: los sprites no aparecían en el escenario de prueba.
- Había concluido que el motor no dibujaba el plano y lo cambió por un cubo de 1 m de grosor. Era un diagnóstico equivocado.
- La causa real era del escenario de prueba, no del plugin: el suelo, la pared y los obstáculos se creaban todos en el origen, y la pared tapaba los clips. Lo encontré y lo corregí a mano en seis corridas cortas.
- Lo demás que hizo Muse en esa tanda sí sirve: el pivote, los 18 hallazgos de Sol, la limpieza de color y el desvanecido de la explosión.

**Estado ahora**
- **Tests:** 15 en verde.
- **Horneado:** los cuatro clips (fuego, columna de humo con fuego, explosión, fuego arcano) salen en unos 50 s.
- **Rendimiento:** 8 simulaciones originales cuestan 50,1 ms por fotograma; 8 clips horneados con sus luces, 4,5 ms; el escenario vacío, 4,1 ms.
- **Ray tracing:** el showcase también corre con ray tracing por hardware, activado solo para esa corrida; la configuración del proyecto no cambia.
- **Subido a `main`:** código, clips, GIFs, capturas, README del plugin, GDD v0.35 y el bloque de bitácora.

**En curso**
- Sonnet está corrigiendo los 12 puntos de la segunda revisión de Sol. Dos son importantes: el sprite hereda la escala del actor y el último fotograma de la explosión no queda vacío. Siete son tests demasiado débiles.
- El plugin sigue desactivado en el `.uproject`. Lo activo cuando Sonnet termine y pasen la compilación del juego y la prueba automática completa.
- Ya dejé preparado, sin compilar, un paso de esa prueba que hace aparecer el fuego en el nivel real y saca captura.

**Dos cosas que necesito de ti, sin prisa**

{"message":"All 12 findings are fixed. I found none of them wrong, and nothing is committed (git untouched).

2. FIXED. GBPixelVfxConvert.cpp, ApplyFadeOut: progress is now (k+1)/N and the last faded frame is cleared explicitly, for both Dissolve and Erode. It runs before ComputeLightTrack, so the light reaches 0 on that frame. I updated the comment in GBPixelVfxConvert.h.
3. FIXED. GBPixelVfxConvert.cpp, RecolorSmallColorClusters: Border.Add became Border.AddUnique, so each boundary pixel casts one vote.

8. HysteresisBand adds vanished pixels that must stay gone, a pixel far below the band that must change, and a 50% coverage change that must bypass the hold.
9. ColorClusters now checks both pixels of a speck. It adds a competing majority (5 votes vs 3, where first-neighbour and darkest-neighbour both fail), a vote tie decided by darkness, two adjacent regions that swap colours (needs the original snapshot), and the L-shape case.
10. FadeOut asserts exact masks. Dissolve is 3 faded frames on a 4x4 frame with a pre-transparent pixel. Erode is a 7x7 frame, plain and with a hole in the centre. It also checks that the last frame is empty, a single-frame clip fades to empty, and looped clips are untouched.

## The owner's idea, and the first answer
The owner's prompt (Spanish, 05:5x UTC): *"para esta Game Jam hagamos un plugin de conversión de Niágara y Niágara Fluids a pixel art [...] no debe quedar en simplemente una pixelización del efecto original, sino que quiero que los parámetros modernos de, por ejemplo, un Niagara Fluid se traspasen a una versión pixelada que se comporte exactamente igual pero que se vea pixel art y sea ligero"*.
Translation: "for this jam let's make a plugin that converts Niagara and Niagara Fluids to pixel art [...] it must not be a plain pixelation of the original effect; I want the modern parameters of, say, a Niagara Fluid carried over to a pixel version that behaves exactly the same but looks like pixel art and is light".

The architect's answer was a no to the general converter and a yes to a small one:
- "Behaves exactly the same and is light" contradicts itself: what costs in a Niagara Fluid is the simulation, not the drawing. Either the effect is baked (same look in motion, almost free, no longer reacts) or it is simulated on a smaller grid (still reacts, only somewhat lighter, not identical).
- There is no general parameter translation: every Niagara system is a different graph of modules.
- The strong half of the idea is the other one: fire, smoke and explosions are hard to draw by hand in pixel art, and the game's art rule says all magic is pixel art.

Translation: "let's do the minimal version you suggest. You are the architect. Check the plan with Astra 6 medium through the Codex CLI, review code with Sol 6.1 medium when it makes sense, and use Muse Spark as the implementer through OpenCode. [...] I am going to sleep, do not stop to ask me for permission or questions. This plugin is YOURS [...] what interests me most is Niagara Fluids and ray tracing behaviors."

"Ray tracing behaviors" was not explained and the owner was asleep. The architect read it as: the pixel version must keep behaving like a light source in a ray-traced / Lumen scene (it lights the scene, its light casts shadows, it shows in reflections), and the bake must keep the volume's own shading. payload.last_assistant_message:
El plugin GBPixelVfx está terminado, activado en el juego y subido a `main` (último commit 1c046cb). Ningún hechizo usa todavía los clips y no reempaqueté el juego.

**Qué hay**
- **Clips:** cuatro efectos de Niagara Fluids horneados a pixel art en la paleta del juego: fuego, columna de humo con fuego en la base, explosión y fuego arcano.
- **Luz:** cada clip lleva una luz real que sigue su brillo: ilumina, proyecta sombras y aparece en reflejos. También lo probé con ray tracing por hardware activado solo para esa corrida.
- **Peso:** 8 simulaciones originales cuestan 50,1 ms por fotograma; 8 clips horneados con sus luces, 4,5 ms; el escenario vacío, 4,1 ms. Los cuatro clips ocupan 56 KB en total.
- **En el juego:** en un build de desarrollo, escribir `pvfx.Spawn FluidFire` en la consola pone el clip en el suelo delante del jugador. Valen también `FluidSmoke`, `FluidExplosion` y `FluidArcaneFire`.

**Comprobaciones finales (una vez, con el plugin activado)**
- La compilación del juego (target `Glyphbound`) pasó en 47 s.
- Los 43 tests del juego y los 15 del plugin están en verde.
- El smoke completo corrió limpio, con dos pasos nuevos que hacen aparecer el fuego en la arena y sacan captura.

**Quién hizo qué**
- **Muse Spark:** hizo la implementación base, pero se atascó dos veces en el escenario de prueba; la segunda vez lo detuve tras 2 h 45 min.
- **Yo:** diagnostiqué y corregí a mano el fallo del escenario (la pared se creaba encima de los clips), y ajusté el aspecto de los clips revisando cada hoja.
- **Sol 6.1:** dos revisiones de código, 18 y 12 hallazgos, todos corregidos.
- **Sonnet:** corrigió los 12 de la segunda revisión, con tu permiso de usarlo en lugar de Muse.

**Lo que queda en tus manos**
- **Interpretación de "ray tracing":** lo tomé como que el efecto horneado siga siendo una fuente de luz real. Si querías otra cosa, dímelo.
- **Uso en hechizos:** hay que decidir cuáles usan qué clip, con qué tamaño y con qué intensidad de luz. Las intensidades actuales (60 cd para los fuegos, 40 el humo, 300 la explosión) las elegí para que se notaran en el escenario de prueba; en la arena, de día, se ven suaves.
- **Empaquetado:** el zip actual es anterior al plugin. El chat del rework de interfaz tiene archivos del juego a medio editar, así que no empaqueté para no meter su trabajo a medias.
- **Prueba humana:** nadie ha jugado con el plugin activado; solo corrió la prueba automática.

Para verlo:

The architect's answer was a no to the general converter and a yes to a small one:
- "Behaves exactly the same and is light" contradicts itself: what costs in a Niagara Fluid is the simulation, not the drawing. Either the effect is baked (same look in motion, almost free, no longer reacts) or it is simulated on a smaller grid (still reacts, only somewhat lighter, not identical).
- There is no general parameter translation: every Niagara system is a different graph of modules.
- The strong half of the idea is the other one: fire, smoke and explosions are hard to draw by hand in pixel art, and the game's art rule says all magic is pixel art.

[...] Me voy a dormir, no te detengas a pedirme permisos ni a hacerme preguntas. Este plugin es TUYO [...] lo que más me interesa es los niagara fluids y comportamientos de Ray tracing."*
Translation: "let's do the minimal version you suggest. You are the architect. Check the plan with Astra 6 medium through the Codex CLI, review code with Sol 6.1 medium when it makes sense, and use Muse Spark as the implementer through OpenCode. [...] I am going to sleep, do not stop to ask me for permission or questions. This plugin is YOURS [...] what interests me most is Niagara Fluids and ray tracing behaviors."

"Ray tracing behaviors" was not explained and the owner was asleep. The architect read it as: the pixel version must keep behaving like a light source in a ray-traced / Lumen scene (it lights the scene, its light casts shadows, it shows in reflections), and the bake must keep the volume's own shading. El Fireball ya usa el fuego horneado y está subido a `main` (commit 9c07f7f). Pasaron las dos compilaciones, los 43 tests del juego, los 15 del plugin y el smoke completo (192 pasos). Nadie lo ha jugado todavía y el juego sigue sin reempaquetar.

**Cómo queda**
- **En vuelo:** el proyectil es la llama horneada, centrada en la mira y de cara a la cámara, e ilumina el suelo por donde pasa.
- **Al estallar:** sale la explosión horneada encima de la onda de siempre. El fogonazo dura unos 0,3 s y después queda una nube de humo gris cerca de 1,2 s; en la captura que te envié ya se ve la fase de humo.
- **Sin cambios:** el ataque básico del bastón y los demás hechizos.

**Valores provisionales (en `Spells.json`, entrada del Fireball)**
- `FlightVfxHeight` 110: alto en cm del clip en vuelo.
- `ImpactVfxSize` 1.1: tamaño de la explosión respecto al diámetro del estallido.
- `ImpactVfxRate` 2: velocidad de la explosión (dura 1,5 s en vez de 3).
- Borrando las líneas `FlightVfx` o `ImpactVfx` vuelve el aspecto anterior de cada parte.

**Cambio en el plugin que afecta a todos los clips**
- El brillo ahora se aplica solo a los píxeles de fuego. Antes aclaraba también el humo hasta dejarlo casi blanco; ahora el humo conserva el gris oscuro de la paleta.

**Avisos**
- **Lo compilado no es exactamente lo subido:** las comprobaciones corrieron con el trabajo sin terminar del chat de la interfaz en el disco. Subí dos archivos compartidos (`Glyphbound.Build.cs` y `GBDevCommands.cpp`) solo con mis líneas, así que esa combinación exacta no se compiló por separado. Mis líneas solo usan funciones que ya estaban subidas, pero si alguien compila `main` limpio y falla, hay que mirar ahí primero.
- **El plugin ya no es opcional:** el juego depende de él, así que no se puede desactivar sin quitar esto del Fireball.
- **Otras máquinas:** los materiales del plugin no están en git. En una máquina que no sea CENTRAL hay que correr `Tools/Jam/PixelVfx-Jam.ps1 -Action Materials` una vez antes de empaquetar.
